statement: A standard interval of length $n\geq0$ is the thin category on $\{0,\ldots,n\}$ freely generated by exactly one directed edge between each successive pair of vertices.
notes: The categorical partial order and the external numerical total order are different structures.

statement: For each $1\leq i\leq n$, exactly one of $i-1\to i$ and $i\to i-1$ is a transition arrow $\underline u_i$.
gap_or_error: The first displayed alternatives in the sentence are indexed i,i+1; the edition itself supplies the correct i-1,i.
repair: Read the bracketed editorial correction; retain both printed readings.

statement: The transition arrows generate all arrows of the standard interval.
notes: Together with thinness and the path graph, this also gives freeness: there are no two different directed paths with the same endpoints.

statement: A transition arrow is direct or retrograde according as its direction agrees or disagrees with the numerical ordering; its sign is respectively + or -.
Standard intervals of length n are classified by words in $\{+,-\}^n$; there are $2^n$ of them.
repair: A sign word determines its free path category, which is thin because the underlying graph is a line.

statement: The source and target of a standard interval are its numerically first and last vertices, 0 and n; its orientation is this total order.
notes: Source and target here are marked endpoints, not necessarily initial and terminal objects of the category.

statement: For $E\subseteq\mathbf Z$, adjacency-connected components are equivalence classes generated by $i\sim i+1$ whenever both integers belong to E; i<j lie in one class iff $[i,j]\subseteq E$.
A chain of transition arrows is a numerically contiguous subset of $\{\underline u_1,\ldots,\underline u_n\}$; its length is its cardinality; the empty subset is allowed by the stated convention.
notes: The explicit indexing formula and the later formula for the domain assume a nonempty chain. A length-zero interval is treated separately.

statement: A nonempty chain is composable iff all its transition signs agree, with the composition ordered appropriately for its direction.
notes: The edition explicitly supplies the reversed composition order in the retrograde case.

statement: The components of the positive and negative transition sets are exactly the maximal composable chains; they partition the transitions and inherit a total order.
The useful length r is the number of maximal composable chains. For n>0, $1\leq r\leq n$; for n=0, r=0.
notes: The zero case is made explicit on manuscript page 5; initial and final directions are undefined there.

statement: Consecutive maximal composable chains have opposite signs. Initial and final directions are respectively the signs of the first and last chains, and agree iff r is odd.
As printed: composable chains correspond to full simplex subcategories, and maximal chains of length i correspond exactly to object-injective functors $\Delta_i\to I$.
gap_or_error: An injective simplex may omit intermediate vertices; it need not be maximal. In $\Delta_2$, the embedding $\Delta_1\to\Delta_2$ with image {0,2} is a counterexample to both identifications with the previously defined contiguous chains.
repair: Object-injective simplices correspond to nonempty finite totally ordered subsets of one structural interval. The contiguous image condition recovers chains, and the whole structural-interval image condition recovers maximal chains.
notes: The full-faithfulness assertion in the next sentence is correct and is audited separately.

statement: Every object-injective functor $\Delta_i\to I$ is fully faithful and monic, and on vertices is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing in the numerical order.
repair: For i>0 all image vertices are pairwise comparable, hence lie in one structural interval, where the categorical order is numerical or reversed. Thinness gives full faithfulness. For i=0 the monotonicity statement is vacuous.

statement: The simplex category $\Delta_i$ is an interval of length i and useful length 1 for i>0, or 0 for i=0. An abstract interval is a category isomorphic to a standard interval.

Proposition 1(a): for n>0, a vertex is a numerical endpoint iff one of $I/i$ and $i\backslash I$ is terminal as a category (one object and its identity) and the other is a nontrivial linearly ordered category $\Delta_j$.
gap_or_error: The later branch diagram labels both branch lengths by r despite the text defining r and s.
repair: Use i+s for the right endpoint of that diagram; the argument distinguishes an endpoint from a non-endpoint source or sink by the two nonempty branches.

statement: The unfinished sentence after Proposition 1(a) asks for a characterization of the designated source endpoint using $i\backslash I$.
gap_or_error: The source sentence is incomplete in the edition; a category without an orientation does not in general select one endpoint.
repair: Do not complete the sentence as a theorem. An orientation, equivalently a choice of endpoint, supplies the missing structure; symmetric intervals prevent an invariant choice.

statement: Proposition 1(b), literally: every endofunctor of an interval fixing both endpoints is the identity.
gap_or_error: On $\Delta_2$, the monotone vertex map $(0,1,2)\mapsto(0,0,2)$ fixes both endpoints and is not the identity.
repair: Replace endofunctor by automorphism for the assertion actually proved by intrinsic reconstruction. Alternatively retain all endofunctors and assume that the interval is reduced; this is an if-and-only-if condition proved in our development after manuscript page 12.

statement: The automorphism group of a nontrivial interval has at most two elements; a nonidentity automorphism exchanges its endpoints. The interval is called symmetric when such an automorphism exists.
gap_or_error: It does not follow from the false endofunctor statement as printed, but the subsequent intrinsic-order argument proves precisely the needed automorphism statement.
repair: An isomorphism preserves indecomposable nonidentity arrows, whose undirected graph is a path. A path automorphism is the identity or reversal.

statement: The underlying interval category together with a chosen endpoint determines the numerical order and therefore the unique oriented identification with a standard interval.
gap_or_error: The inductive paragraph prints $i\backslash I,I/i$ although the construction is in the remaining full tail $I\prime$ at its endpoint $s_i$.
repair: Read $s_i\backslash I\prime,I\prime/s_i$ in that paragraph; or use successive neighbours in the indecomposable-arrow path graph.

statement: Proposition 2: for every standard interval I there is a unique standard interval I′ and isomorphism $\theta:I\to I′$ exchanging source and target; on vertices $\theta(i)=n-i$.
repair: The new sign word is $(-\varepsilon_n,\ldots,-\varepsilon_1)$. The length-zero case is the identity.

statement: The orientation-opposite interval $I^{\mathrm{opp}}$ has the same underlying category as I and the reverse external total order.

A nontrivial abstract interval has precisely two oriented standard presentations; choosing an orientation is equivalent to choosing its source endpoint. Their standard models coincide iff the category is symmetric.
The categorical opposite $I^o$ is an interval obtained by changing every transition sign while retaining the vertex numbering.
notes: This operation is distinct from reversing the external orientation.

statement: The three-vertex span and cospan are symmetric but are opposite nonisomorphic categories; every $\Delta_i$ is self-dual and has trivial automorphism group.
repair: The span has one initial and two maximal vertices, the cospan two minimal and one terminal vertex; the ordered simplex is self-dual by reversal.

statement: For n>0 any isomorphism $I\to I^o$ is the vertex reversal, is unique, and forces the first and last signs to agree. Symmetry forces those signs to disagree, so the two properties cannot coexist.
notes: The full criteria are palindromicity and opposite-palindromicity respectively. The edition adds a length-zero qualification; our commentary handles the point separately.

statement: The two oriented versions of the simplex are denoted $\Delta_i^+$ and $\Delta_i^-$ for i>0.
The domain of a nonempty chain of l transitions beginning at index i is the full numerical interval $[i-1,i+l-1]$.
notes: The empty-chain convention on manuscript page 3 does not give a uniquely positioned domain; the formula is used here for nonempty chains.

statement: Structural or critical intervals are the vertex domains of maximal composable chains. Their lengths are the run lengths $l_1,\ldots,l_r$; adjacent intervals share one endpoint and nonadjacent interiors are disjoint.
gap_or_error: The comparison sentence prints each element of I instead of each element of $I_i$.
repair: Read $I_i$ in that comparison; leave the printed slip unchanged in the source.

statement: A critical vertex is an endpoint of a structural interval: for n>0, the numerical endpoints together with every index where consecutive signs change.
Proposition 3 as printed: with $A=(I/s)\setminus\{s\}$ and $B=(s\backslash I)\setminus\{s\}$, s is critical iff $I\setminus\{s\}=A\amalg B$.
gap_or_error: A and B need not contain vertices incomparable to s. In $0\to1\leftarrow2$, the critical endpoint s=0 has A empty and B={1}, whereas deleting s also leaves vertex 2.
repair: Replace $I\setminus\{s\}$ by the full subcategory on $(\operatorname{Ob}(I/s)\cup\operatorname{Ob}(s\backslash I))\setminus\{s\}$. The footnote criterion, no arrows between A and B, is correct. For deletion in all of I, use the numerical left/right partition instead.

statement: The footnote to Proposition 3: s is critical iff there are no arrows between the strict predecessor category $A=(I/s)\setminus\{s\}$ and strict successor category $B=(s\backslash I)\setminus\{s\}$.
repair: At a critical vertex one of A and B is empty. At an interior noncritical vertex both are nonempty and every composable pair through s yields an arrow from A to B.

statement: Proposition 4: for distinct i<j, the following are equivalent: there is an arrow in one direction between them; they belong to one structural interval; the full category on $[i,j]$ is $\Delta_{j-i}$ up to isomorphism.
repair: The unique underlying path from i to j is directed exactly when all intermediate signs agree; this is exactly containment in one maximal run.

statement: Two objects are directly connected if at least one of the two hom-sets between them is nonempty; a subinterval is a nonempty connected full subcategory of an interval.
notes: Here connectedness is categorical zigzag connectedness, not contiguity of the original numerical vertex subset.

statement: Proposition 5(a): every nonempty connected component of a full subcategory of an interval is itself an interval, with orientation induced by the original numerical order.
gap_or_error: The proof is largely left implicit.
repair: List the chosen vertices increasingly. Consecutive chosen vertices are linked precisely when no omitted critical vertex lies between them. These linked blocks are intervals; there are no arrows between different blocks.

statement: Proposition 5(b): for a vertex subset J with minimum i, maximum j and i<j, its full subcategory is connected iff it contains every critical vertex of I lying in $[i,j]$.
gap_or_error: The text gives the obstruction direction by invoking the inaccurate global formulation of Proposition 3; sufficiency is not written out.
repair: A missing turning vertex separates the numerical left/right parts. If no turning vertex is missing, consecutive chosen vertices are joined by arrows within structural intervals.

statement: Footnote 4, literally: every subcategory of I which is an interval is necessarily full.
gap_or_error: In $\Delta_2$, keep objects 0,1,2 and arrows $0\to1$, $0\to2$ (with identities), but omit $1\to2$. This is a span interval and is not full.
repair: Retain fullness in the definition of subinterval. A sufficient corrected assertion is that an injective functor from an interval which is monotone in the external orientations and has induced interval image is fully faithful; the unrestricted claim is invalid.

statement: If an interior critical vertex of the numerical span of J is omitted, J splits as a coproduct of its nonempty left and right parts.
repair: An arrow crossing the omitted vertex would require a constant sign across it, contradicting criticality. This proves the stated separation without the defective formula in Proposition 3.

statement: The smallest full connected subcategory containing i<j has vertices i, j and all critical vertices strictly between them; in particular the critical vertices form the smallest subinterval containing both endpoints.
An interval is reduced (irredundant) if all its vertices are critical, equivalently each structural run has length one.
notes: Section 2 assumes positive length. We extend the convention to the point by declaring its sole vertex critical.

statement: A positive-length reduced oriented interval is determined by its length n and initial sign; the signs alternate, and its final sign agrees with the initial sign iff n is odd.
Proposition 6: a full subinterval with endpoints i<j is reduced iff each of its other vertices is critical in the ambient interval.
repair: Successive retained vertices lie in structural runs; the two induced transitions at an interior retained vertex change sign exactly when that vertex is an ambient turning point.

statement: The full subcategory on critical vertices is a reduced subinterval, denoted $I_{\mathrm{red}}$.
A path of oriented type I in X is a functor $c:I\to X$, and its category of fixed-type paths is $\operatorname{Fun}(I,X)$.
The chosen orientation supplies a unique standard model, so fixed-type paths may be represented by a sign word of length n.
As printed, the length n of the path is $\operatorname{card} I$.
gap_or_error: The category has n+1 vertices; this contradicts both the initial definition and the immediately following object list.
repair: Read $n=|\operatorname{Ob}I|-1=|\operatorname{Tr}(I)|$. The equality is printed and therefore retained as an edition slip.

statement: A functor $I\to X$ is uniquely specified by n+1 objects and one arrow with the prescribed sign between every successive pair; every such datum extends to a functor.
notes: Generation proves uniqueness; freeness of the path category proves existence. No relation between distinct directed paths must be checked.

statement: A morphism of fixed-type paths is a tuple of vertex maps satisfying the n naturality squares for transition arrows.
repair: Naturality for every longer arrow follows by composing the transition squares, in reverse index order on a retrograde run.

statement: When i<j are joined by an arrow in I, that arrow and its image in X are the composites of the corresponding constant-sign transition chain.
Paths of type $\Delta_0$ and their maps form X; the sole identity of the shape maps to the identity of the selected object.
Paths of type $\Delta_1^+$ form the arrow category of X. Type $\Delta_1^-$ gives the same arrow category with the two endpoint evaluations interchanged.
Types $\Delta_2^+$ and $\Delta_2^-$ describe a composable pair and the same ordered pair read with reversed external orientation.
The types $\Phi_1$ and $\Psi_1$ describe respectively spans $a_0\leftarrow a_1\to a_2$ and cospans $a_0\to a_1\leftarrow a_2$.
notes: The displayed transition labels u_0,u_1 are a local reindexing from the earlier u_1,u_2 convention, and are clearly underlined in the PDF.

statement: The span and cospan categories are nonisomorphic; in general their functor categories into X are not isomorphic.
repair: For X the three-object span, there are 11 span diagrams and 9 cospan diagrams. Both functor categories are posets, so they are not even equivalent. Full counting proof is supplied in the commentary.

statement: Reversing the external orientation of I leaves its underlying functor category canonically isomorphic, but exchanges the source and target of each path.
The intrinsic datum of a path is an orientation together with a functor; its fixed-type category comes equipped with endpoint evaluation $\operatorname{Fun}(I,X)\to X\times X$.
Endpoint evaluation is restriction along the endpoint map $\alpha:\{0,1\}_{\mathrm{disc}}\to I$.
gap_or_error: Calling alpha an inclusion includes an unstated positive-length proviso.
repair: At n=0 it is the fold onto the unique vertex and endpoint evaluation is the diagonal $X\to X\times X$; no formula needs to change.

statement: Orientation reversal commutes with endpoint evaluation after transposing the factors of $X\times X$.
notes: The canonical identity-on-underlying-diagram comparison is generally over the transposition, not over the identity of the endpoint base.

statement: If an interval has an orientation-preserving isomorphism to the same category with opposite orientation, then it is symmetric; this occurs for the span and cospan but not for nontrivial simplices.
notes: The continuation to reduced even length and the distinction between the two resulting path comparisons is on manuscript page 19 and is assigned to the next audit section.

statement: For the full inclusion $j:R=I_{\mathrm{red}}\hookrightarrow I$, the run-source and run-target collapses satisfy $r_t\dashv j\dashv r_s$ and $r_sj=r_tj=\mathrm{id}_R$. Their comparison transformations fix all critical vertices. For every category X, $r_s^*\dashv j^*\dashv r_t^*$ on functor categories; if X is a groupoid, $j^*$ is an equivalence.
repair: Define both retractions to fix critical vertices and send an interior vertex to the categorical source or target of its unique structural run. The only comparable critical vertices are those two endpoints, so thinness gives the natural hom-set bijections. Precomposition reverses the adjunctions; groupoid targets make all comparison components invertible.
references: Riehl2016, Proposition 4.3.7; ArakawaCnossen2026, proof of Lemma 4.16 (known critical-vertex reduction)
notes: Commentators' development, marked \ours in the block The critical-vertex inclusion has two adjoints; not attributed to Grothendieck. The point is explicitly treated by taking its sole vertex as critical and both retractions as identities. The additional adjoint formulas are supplied here without a priority claim; the underlying reduction and general precomposition calculus are known.

statement: A finite oriented interval I is reduced if and only if every endofunctor $f:I\to I$ fixing its two designated endpoints is the identity; the point is included as reduced.
repair: For a reduced interval of length n, every nonidentity target arrow is a transition, so $|f(i)-f(i-1)|\leq1$. Fixed endpoints force the sum of the n differences to equal n, hence every difference is 1 and f is the identity. If I is not reduced, the nonidentity source-collapse $jr_s$ fixes every critical vertex and thus both endpoints.
references: Commentary after manuscript p.12, The exact scope of endpoint rigidity; VIIa-A060 for the source-collapse construction
notes: Commentators' development, marked \ours; a sharp repair of the false printed Proposition 1(b), not a claim made by Grothendieck. The functor is arbitrary: numerical monotonicity is proved from equality and is not an extra hypothesis. No priority claim is made.

statement: Every nontrivial reduced interval of even length is symmetric; an isomorphism of oriented intervals induces an isomorphism of their path categories compatible with both endpoint evaluations.
repair: For alternating sign words of even length, reversal of vertices reverses the sign sequence in precisely the required way. Precomposition with the inverse isomorphism preserves the named endpoints.
notes: Continuation of the two distinct reversal operations discussed on ms.18; do not confuse reversal of orientation with opposite category.

statement: A path type is a finite sign word \tau, represented by its canonically oriented standard interval I_\tau; choosing this representative eliminates ambiguity from presentations of an unoriented interval.
notes: This does not say that X^{I_\tau} has no automorphisms; it concerns the indexing convention.

statement: For finite intervals I,J, natural transformations of set-valued functors Cat(I,-)\Rightarrow Cat(J,-) are in bijection with functors J\to I, by \varphi\mapsto(c\mapsto c\varphi).
repair: Explicit universal-path proof in the p20 commentary: evaluate the transformation at id_I and use naturality with respect to c:I\to X.
notes: The source invokes Yoneda; preserve the reverse variance. Two underlined Ch symbols caused by the supplied macro conflict are corrected in the transcription.

statement: The operation (a_0\xrightarrow{u}a_1\xrightarrow{v}a_2)\mapsto(a_0\xrightarrow{vu}a_2) is represented by the endpoint map [1]\to[2]; insertion of a final identity after composition is represented by (0,1,2)\mapsto(0,2,2).
repair: Functorial action on natural transformations and idempotence of the second operation are computed in the p23 example.

statement: An interval category is thin; a functor category between two interval categories is thin, so every diagram in such a category commutes.
repair: Components of a natural transformation lie in singleton-or-empty hom-sets; existence is pointwise comparability, and all naturality equations then hold automatically.
notes: The assertion is about interval targets, not about arbitrary categories of paths X^I.

statement: Every universal object-level path operation classified above extends canonically to a functor X^I\to X^J by whiskering natural transformations with the representing functor J\to I.
repair: Components (v\varphi)_j=v_{\varphi(j)} preserve identities, composition, and naturality; full verification in p20 commentary.
notes: The printed id_C in L(id_C) is a capitalization slip; read id_c, but retain the edition.

statement: The remaining construction programme consists of organizing all path shapes into one category, defining concatenation, and developing only the interval morphism theory needed for those constructions.
notes: A programme, not a theorem or a claim of an open research problem.

statement: The set Ty of path types is the free monoid on the two one-edge types + and -, with the empty word as unit.
repair: Words may repeat signs. Only their successive maximal constant-sign blocks alternate.
notes: Initial and final signs are undefined for the empty word.

statement: Every nonempty type has a unique decomposition \varepsilon_1^{l_1}\cdots\varepsilon_r^{l_r}, with l_i>0 and \varepsilon_{i+1}=-\varepsilon_i; r is its useful length and the l_i are the lengths of its critical intervals.
repair: Take the maximal consecutive blocks of equal signs; maximality gives uniqueness.

statement: The initial category of types has sign words as objects and all functors I_\tau\to I_{\tau'} as morphisms, composed as functors.
notes: This first category is later renamed Typ. Footnote 7 anticipates the subsequent endpoint restriction; it is not the final definition of Ty.

statement: For any two types the functor category Hom(I_\tau,I_{\tau'}) is a poset, endowing the hom-set of the initial type category with an order.
repair: An interval is a poset, so natural transformations exist at most uniquely; mutual comparability gives pointwise equality of object functions and hence of functors.

statement: Realization \tau\mapsto I_\tau is fully faithful from the category with all interval functors to Cat; it is generally only faithful after imposing endpoint preservation.
repair: Fullness is tautological for the first definition; footnote 8 correctly withdraws it for the revised category. The p25 block separates T_all, T_boundary, and T_increasing.
notes: No uncorrected contradiction: the assertion and its retraction refer to successive definitions.

statement: For each category X, precomposition makes F_X(\tau)=Fun(I_\tau,X) into a strict functor T^{op}\to Cat for each selected category T of types.
repair: (\varphi\psi)^*=\psi^*\varphi^* and 1^*=1 hold literally.

statement: The Grothendieck construction of F_X is a split fibration \pi_X:Ch_T(X)\to T, whose fiber at \tau is Fun(I_\tau,X).
repair: Complete construction and Cartesian-lift verification in p27 commentary.
notes: No opfibration is claimed in the source; the p28 example demonstrates why that stronger property would require additional colimits.

statement: An arrow from (\tau',c') to (\tau,c) over \varphi:\tau'\to\tau is exactly a natural transformation v:c'\Rightarrow c\varphi.
The composite of (\varphi,v) and (\varphi',v') is (\varphi\varphi',(v\varphi')\circ v'); identities are (1,1), and these operations define a category.
repair: Componentwise associativity and identity verification in p27 commentary.

repair: In general no: take X=I_+, the shape map e->I_+ selecting vertex1, and its universal Cartesian lift. Source evaluation would require an arrow 1->0 in I_+, which does not exist. Restricting shape maps to endpoint-preserving maps resolves the source's question.

statement: To obtain the endpoint arrows by the components v_{0_{\tau'}} and v_{1_{\tau'}}, with no further comparison arrows, it suffices and universally is necessary that \varphi preserve the specified endpoints.
repair: Necessity for literal component evaluation is tested on X=I_\tau,c=id. The p29 development distinguishes this from a larger class allowing canonical endpoint comparison arrows.

repair: Complete necessity, closure under composition, sufficiency, and uniqueness proof in the development block 'How much endpoint preservation is forced'.
references: GrothendieckSGA1, Expose VI, Proposition 12.1; Riehl2016, Theorem 2.2.4

statement: The intermediate category T_boundary has the same objects as Typ and only functors preserving source and target; equivalently it is the full subcategory of epsilon\Cat on the pointed interval objects epsilon\to I_\tau.
repair: For the empty type epsilon\to I_e is not injective; interpret the displayed hooks as structure maps in that case.

statement: The endpoint-preserving path category is the strict base change of the unrestricted Grothendieck construction: Ch(X)\cong CH(X)\times_{Typ}T_boundary.
repair: Both constructions have identical objects and identical pairs (\varphi,v) precisely for the restricted set of \varphi; composition agrees.

statement: The total path categories depend functorially on X, including categories large relative to a smaller universe.
repair: Postcompose paths and natural transformations with X\to Y. Use nested universes U in V: the type category is U-small and X may be V-small; p27 commentary makes the convention explicit.

statement: The proposed category of paths should support both the fraction construction M Sigma^{-1} and composition of paths.

references: GabrielZisman1967, I.1.1-I.1.2; DwyerKan1980Calculating, Definition 2.1 and Propositions 2.2, 3.1
notes: Design tests, not assertions that the general existence of localization is presently open.

statement: For the intermediate endpoint category the horizontal maps T_boundary\to epsilon\Cat and Typ\to Cat in the displayed square are fully faithful.
repair: Both are full by their definitions at this stage. After the further monotonicity restriction, the first is no longer generally full.
notes: Example distinguishing the stages: I_{+-+}\to I_+ with vertex sequence (0,1,0,1).

statement: The final category Ty retains precisely the endpoint-preserving functors whose object functions are nondecreasing in the external order of interval vertices.
notes: The external progression order differs from the categorical partial order. Subsequent text temporarily studies arbitrary endpoint maps as well.

statement: The critical intervals K_1,...,K_r glue along successive endpoint vertices to give I_\tau; functors I_\tau\to I_{\tau'} are exactly families of functors K_i\to I_{\tau'} agreeing at shared vertices.
repair: Universal-property proof from the unique transition-path factorization of each arrow is supplied in p32 commentary. For source e treat its unique vertex separately.

statement: Such a glued functor preserves both endpoints exactly when the first component sends the source to the target source and the last sends the target to the target endpoint.
repair: The endpoint values are those of the first and last component. The formulation with first/last component assumes nonempty source; the empty source admits an endpoint map only to e.

statement: If a nondegenerate target interval has a subset J of pairwise comparable vertices, J is contained in a critical interval; this interval is unique when J has at least two distinct vertices.
gap_or_error: The footnote omits the nondegenerate-target exception: I_e has no critical intervals, even for its singleton vertex set.

statement: A functor from a chain interval into a nondegenerate interval has its image in one critical interval; if nonconstant this interval is unique, and its vertex function is increasing or decreasing according as the two interval signs agree or disagree.
repair: Images of chain vertices are pairwise comparable; apply the previous lemma and translate categorical order into external order. Target e gives the unique constant map.

statement: A constant functor at every non-endpoint vertex of a target interval factors through exactly two critical intervals.
gap_or_error: Printed overstatement: an interior vertex of a long constant-sign run lies in only one critical interval.
repair: Replace 'non-endpoint vertex' by 'interior critical vertex'. The constant map to 1 in I_{++} is a counterexample to the printed form. Endpoints and noncritical vertices lie in one run, interior critical vertices in two, and the point interval has no runs.
notes: Retain the printed text; this is not a transcription error. Does not affect Proposition 7.

statement: Proposition 7: If f:I_\tau\to I_{\tau'} is any functor and K is a source critical interval on which f is nonconstant, exactly one target critical interval contains f(K). If f is nondecreasing, the two intervals have the same sign.
repair: Apply the preceding chain-image argument; p32 commentary supplies the complete minimum/maximum and sign calculation.

statement: If s_0,...,s_r are the source critical vertices, the full subcategory on their image vertices t_i=f(s_i) is connected, hence is a subinterval in the sense of a connected full subcategory.
repair: Consecutive t_i are comparable, since source critical intervals are chains.
notes: For a point source, one may take its sole vertex as the separate degenerate case.

statement: For increasing f, the full subcategory on the image critical vertices equals the ambient integer interval [f(s_0),f(s_r)].
gap_or_error: The image set may skip noncritical vertices, even for f=id on I_{++}; its critical-image set is {0,2}, not {0,1,2}.
repair: It has those least/greatest vertices and that order-convex hull, and contains all target critical vertices lying in the hull. The p34 block gives the exact distinction.
notes: The false equality is printed in the edition. All subsequent critical-vertex coverage assertions survive.

statement: For any functor and critical source vertices s_i,s_j, every target critical vertex between f(s_i) and f(s_j) equals f(s_k) for some k between i and j.
gap_or_error: The corollary mistakenly calls s_i,s_j vertices of I_{\tau'} instead of I_\tau.
repair: Use the finite sequence f(s_i),...,f(s_j): it cannot cross a target turn strictly between two consecutive comparable values. Full proof in p34 commentary.

statement: If f preserves endpoints, f(Ob I_{\tau,red}) contains Ob I_{\tau',red}.
repair: Apply critical-vertex coverage to the two source endpoints; for target e the degenerate case is immediate.
notes: This is a containment of vertex sets, not a factorization of f through a reduced target.

statement: An increasing endpoint-preserving functor need not take every source critical vertex to a target critical vertex.
repair: The source's map I_{+-+}\to I_{++} has vertex sequence (0,1,1,2); the two middle critical vertices go to the noncritical target vertex 1.

statement: Cr(\tau) is the linearly ordered set of source critical intervals; it is canonically order-isomorphic to the transition set of the reduced interval.
notes: Empty when \tau=e.

statement: Cr(\tau,f) is the subset of source critical intervals on which f is nonconstant; Proposition 7 defines a function Cr(\tau,f)\to Cr(\tau').
notes: For endpoint maps it is subsequently denoted Cr(f).

statement: Corollary 2(a): For any functor of intervals, the image of Cr(\tau,f)\to Cr(\tau') is an order-convex subset of the set of target critical intervals, possibly empty.
